The flux in an iron core changes at 0.2 Wb/s. A secondary coil of 50 turns has an induced voltage of

Rule: Faraday's law: v = N ΔΦ / Δt.
Apply: 50 × 0.2 = 10 V.
Check: 0.004 V divides, 250 V uses N / rate, and 1 V forgets the turns.
Which core is the better choice for a 50 Hz mains transformer?
Iron core, because it links almost all the flux
Air core, because it has no loss
Plastic core, because it is light

Rule: iron has a high permeability.
Apply: the primary and secondary windings share almost all the flux, so k ≈ 1 at low frequency.
Check: air-core types are for high frequency, plastic and no core give very weak coupling.
The primary of a transformer carries steady DC. The secondary voltage is
zero, because the flux does not change

Rule: a voltage is induced only while the flux changes.
Apply: a steady current gives a constant flux, so v = N ΔΦ / Δt = 0.
Check: the other answers need a changing flux.
An audio amplifier uses a transformer. The core is most likely

Rule: iron-core transformers are used in audio circuits and power systems.
Apply: an audio signal is at low frequency, so iron gives good coupling.
Check: air cores are used at radio frequencies.
N_P = 200, N_S = 800 and V_P = 24 V. The secondary voltage is

Rule: V_S = n V_P with n = N_S / N_P.
Apply: n = 800 / 200 = 4, so V_S = 4 × 24 = 96 V (step-up).
Check: 6 V divides by 4, 24 V ignores n, and 4 V is just n.
A secondary of 24 V end to end has a center tap. The voltage from one end to the tap is

Rule: a center tap splits the secondary into two equal halves.
Apply: 24 V / 2 = 12 V on each half.
Check: 24 V is the whole winding, 48 V doubles it, 6 V halves it twice.
A 230 V primary has 1000 turns. A secondary tap at 200 turns gives

Rule: each tap has its own turns ratio, V = V_P N / N_P.
Apply: 230 × 200 / 1000 = 46 V.
Check: 11.5 V is the 50-turn tap, 230 V is the primary, 1150 V uses 5000 turns.
An auto-transformer has 400 turns across 230 V. A tap at 100 turns gives

Rule: the voltage is shared in proportion to the turns of the one winding.
Apply: 230 × 100 / 400 = 57.5 V.
Check: 920 V inverts the ratio, 23 V uses 40 turns, 115 V uses 200 turns.
Compared with a two-winding transformer, an auto-transformer is

Rule: one winding serves as both primary and secondary.
Apply: less copper is needed, so it is smaller and lighter.
Check: it does change the voltage by tapping the winding.
A variable transformer is used when
the output voltage must be set smoothly from zero up to the maximum
the output voltage must stay fixed

Rule: an adjustable transformer has a sliding contact on the winding.
Apply: moving the contact changes the number of turns, so the output voltage changes.
Check: a fixed output needs fixed taps, DC cannot be transformed, and an antenna needs matching, not adjusting.
In an auto-transformer, the single winding is
shared by the primary and the secondary

Rule: an auto-transformer has one winding for both sides.
Apply: the primary uses the whole winding and the secondary uses a part of it.
Check: a winding cannot be limited to one side, and no magnet is used.
A source has Z_S = 400 Ω and the load is 4 Ω. The turns ratio for maximum power is

Rule: n = √(Z_L / Z_S).
Apply: √(4 / 400) = √0.01 = 0.1.
Check: 0.01 forgets the square root, 10 and 100 invert the ratio.
A transformer with n = 0.1 connects a 4 Ω speaker to an amplifier. The amplifier sees

Rule: Z_P = Z_L / n².
Apply: 4 / 0.1² = 4 / 0.01 = 400 Ω.
Check: 40 Ω divides by n only, 0.04 Ω multiplies by n², 4 Ω ignores the transformer.
Maximum power is delivered to a load when
the load impedance equals the source impedance
the load is much larger than the source

Rule: maximum power transfer needs a match, Z_L = Z_S.
Apply: a transformer with the right n makes the load look equal to the source.
Check: a zero load or a very large load gives little power, and n = 1 matches only equal impedances.
